```bash
kubectl run -i --tty --rm prisma \
  --image registry.ic-ops.net/internal-tooling/churn-renewal-forecast:latest \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"prisma","image":"registry.ic-ops.net/internal-tooling/churn-renewal-forecast:latest","stdin":true,"tty":true,"envFrom":[{"secretRef":{"name":"churn-renewal-forecast"}}]}]}}' \
  -- /bin/bash
```

The `--overrides` JSON patches the pod spec directly, using `envFrom` + `secretRef` to load every key in the `churn-renewal-forecast` secret as an env var. The `stdin: true` and `tty: true` fields are required to keep the `-i --tty` behavior working alongside the override.

content.text:
Found the root cause. There's no `prisma/migrations/` directory — the project has only ever used `db:push`. The migrate job runs `prisma migrate deploy`, which looks for migration files in `prisma/migrations/`. With no folder there, it has nothing to apply and skips creating tables entirely.

The fix is to generate the initial migration from the current schema:

```bash
bunx prisma migrate dev --name init
```

This creates `prisma/migrations/<timestamp>_init/migration.sql` with all the `CREATE TABLE` statements. Commit that folder and the migrate job will have something to actually run.

One gotcha: if your local DB already has tables from `db:push`, Prisma will detect drift and complain. If that happens:

```bash
# Option A: reset local DB and let migration recreate everything
bunx prisma migrate reset

# Option B: generate the SQL without applying it, then baseline the existing DB
bunx prisma migrate dev --name init --create-only
bunx prisma migrate resolve --applied <generated-migration-name>
```

Option B is safer if you have local data you want to keep — it marks the migration as already applied without touching the DB, then future migrations run normally.

After that, also add a `db:migrate` script to `package.json` so the migrate job has a clean entrypoint:

```json
"db:migrate": "prisma migrate deploy"
```

You don't even need to change `db.ts` for this. The `pg` library respects libpq environment variables — so if you bake the cert into the image and set `PGSSLMODE` + `PGSSLROOTCERT` as env vars, SSL gets negotiated automatically with no code changes.

**1. Add the cert to the Dockerfile**

```dockerfile
# In the runner stage, fetch the RDS CA bundle
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && \
    curl -o /etc/ssl/certs/rds-ca-bundle.pem \
    https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/global/global-bundle.pem && \
    apt-get remove -y curl && apt-get autoclean
```

Or `COPY` it in if you'd rather not fetch at build time (check it into the repo under `deploy/certs/`).

**2. Set env vars in the configmap**

```
PGSSLMODE=verify-full
PGSSLROOTCERT=/etc/ssl/certs/rds-ca-bundle.pem
```

That's it — no `db.ts` changes, no `DATABASE_URL` tweaks. Both the web app (`pg`) and the migration job (Prisma Rust engine) respect these libpq env vars, so both get SSL with full cert verification.

You can also revert the `db.ts` change I made earlier since it's no longer needed.

content.text:
The bugbot is misreading the intent here. These are two different schemas for two different purposes:

- **`pgboss` schema** — pg-boss's own internal tables (`job`, `schedule`, etc.). Pg-boss always qualifies its table names with its own schema, so it doesn't need the `search_path` change.
- **`churn_forecast` schema** — application tables (`SyncJob`, `Contract`, etc.) that Prisma queries. This is what the `search_path` fix in `getDatabaseUrl()` addresses.

Wiring `DATABASE_SCHEMA` into the pg-boss connection would actually break things — pg-boss would try to resolve unqualified references against `churn_forecast` instead of its expected `pgboss` schema.

The split is intentional and correct. You can dismiss that finding.

OK so now it clicks, fr fr. The key insight from Haris: the PrivateLink endpoint service already fronts the nginx NLB, and nginx routes by hostname. The endpoint doesn't care which hostname is requested — it just forwards TCP to the NLB, and nginx does the routing. So `churn-forecast.ic-ops.net` traffic would work fine through the existing endpoint.

The VPN problem is pure DNS: from VPN-connected VPCs, `argocd.ic-ops.net` resolves to the **endpoint ENI IPs** (via the PrivateLink private DNS override), while `churn-forecast.ic-ops.net` resolves to the raw NLB IPs (from the public zone / external-dns record) — which aren't reachable from VPN directly.

The fix: in the `ic-ops.net` private hosted zone, add a CNAME record:

```
churn-forecast.ic-ops.net → CNAME → argocd.ic-ops.net
```

When a VPN-connected VPC resolves `churn-forecast.ic-ops.net`, it follows the CNAME to `argocd.ic-ops.net`, which then gets the private DNS override → endpoint ENI IPs → traffic flows through the existing endpoint → NLB → nginx → your app.

So the `churn-forecast-privatelink` module doesn't need the `networking-privatelink-service-provider` module at all. It just needs a single Route53 CNAME record.
